Figure 1:Overview ofBridgeWAM.Left: LIBERO-Plus success rates and parameters.
Center: LBQs replace dense MoT video K/V, linking 30-layer Video and two-layer Action Experts.
Right: real-world manipulation tasks, success rates, and measured inference latency in evaluated settings.

Figure 2:Comparison of the BoE and MoT architectures.BoE uses Latent Bridge Queries (LBQs) to transfer action-relevant visual features between experts.
Unlike MoT’s matched-depth coupling, BoE decouples expert depths, enablingBridgeWAMto use only two layers in the Action DiT while retaining the full Video Expert for learning rich representations of visual information.

Figure 3:Overview of the BridgeWAM architecture.Latent Bridge Queries (LBQs) first aggregate action-relevant representations from the Video DiT and are read by the
Action DiT to guide action prediction, forming a compact bridge through which information flows from video to action.

Figure 4:Real-world manipulation tasks and results.We compareπ0.5\pi_{0.5}, Fast-WAM, andBridgeWAMon closing a laptop
and picking and placing a drink, a pen, and a mouse.
The task panels show the original settings and variations in object
height, type, color, position, or count, together with success rates (%).
The right panels summarize success rates and inference latency (ms).

Figure 5:Action-conditioned visual routing maps.The top row shows Fast-WAM attention averaged across Video-DiT layers,
while the bottom row shows the LBQ-mediated routing at the final Video-DiT layer ofBridgeWAM.
The columns show the models under variations in background texture, lighting, camera viewpoint,
robot initial state, object layout, and sensor noise.

Figure 6:Frame-by-frame comparisons on real-robot tasks.The four panels show closing a laptop and picking and placing a drink,
a pen, and a mouse. Each panel compares Fast-WAM (upper row) withBridgeWAM(lower row), with the sequence of frames progressing from left to right.

Figure 7:Additional visual routing examples: bowl placement.The tasks place a black bowl onto a plate from the stove (upper panel)
or the cookie box (lower panel). Within each comparison, the results from Fast-WAM are shown above the corresponding results fromBridgeWAM.

Figure 8:Additional visual routing examples: basket placement.The tasks place butter (upper panel) or salad dressing (lower panel)
into a basket. Within each comparison, the results from Fast-WAM are shown above the corresponding results fromBridgeWAM.

Figure 9:Additional visual routing examples: different placement goals.The tasks place ketchup into a basket (upper panel) and a wine bottle
on top of a cabinet (lower panel). In each comparison, the Fast-WAM results are shown above the results forBridgeWAM.
